intro.t: Watch for teachers who make things up.
b: A warning against false teaching and against scoffers who use the delay of Christ's return as an argument. The delay, Peter says, is patience, not absence.

1.t: The Greek construction here matches four others in this short letter that are rendered of one person. Worth comparing 1:11, 2:20, 3:2 and 3:18.
Peter appeals to what he saw at the transfiguration, then says the prophetic word is more certain still. Verse 21 on how Scripture came about is foundational.

3.t: The delay is patience, not absence. A day is as a thousand years — a statement about God's relation to time, used pastorally.

2.t: A fierce chapter, parallel to Jude. The marks given are exploitation, sensuality and greed — conduct rather than only doctrine.

1.ctx: Peter writes what he presents as his final letter, knowing his death is near (1:14). Its authorship has been more widely questioned than any other New Testament book.
1.mean: Peter greets those who have obtained a faith of equal standing by the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
1.big: Peter's greeting calls Jesus Christ both God and Saviour.
1.diff: Many scholars doubt Peter wrote this letter, citing its style and its apparent knowledge of Paul's letters as Scripture (3:16). Others, including many evangelical scholars, defend Petrine authorship, possibly with a different secretary. The church accepted it as Scripture after some hesitation. In verse 1 the Greek construction most naturally reads as one person, 'our God and Saviour', a direct statement of Christ's deity.

1.ctx: The letter's main positive teaching, against false teachers who treated grace as permission to sin.
1.mean: Peter says God's divine power has granted all things for life and godliness, and through his promises believers become partakers of the divine nature. So they must make every effort to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection and love. Be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election.
1.big: Having been given everything by God, believers must make every effort to grow in godliness.
1.diff: 'Partakers of the divine nature' has been understood very differently: Eastern Orthodox theology builds on it a doctrine of theosis (becoming like God by grace); Reformed and evangelical theology understands it as sharing God's moral character through union with Christ, not becoming divine in essence.

1.ctx: Peter defends the reliability of the apostolic message about Christ's return.
1.mean: Peter says they did not follow cleverly devised myths, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty when he received honour and glory from the Father on the holy mountain. And they have the prophetic word more fully confirmed. No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation; men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.big: The apostles' message rests on eyewitness testimony and on Scripture inspired by the Holy Spirit.
1.diff: Verses 20–21 are a foundational text for the doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture, alongside 2 Timothy 3:16.

2.ctx: A long warning closely parallel to Jude, from which it probably draws. The false teachers claimed Christian freedom meant freedom from moral restraint.
2.mean: Peter says false teachers will arise among them, even denying the Master who bought them. He cites God's judgement on angels who sinned, on the ancient world in the flood, and on Sodom and Gomorrah, while rescuing Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and keep the unrighteous under punishment. The false teachers are bold, greedy and sensual, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. It would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness.
2.big: God will judge false teachers who exploit the church, and will rescue those who belong to him.
2.diff: Verse 1 ('denying the Master who bought them') is discussed in debates about the extent of the atonement, and verses 20–22 in debates about whether true believers can fall away. Reformed interpreters generally read them as describing those who professed faith without genuine conversion.

3.ctx: The false teachers mocked the promise of Christ's return because it had not yet happened.
3.mean: Peter says scoffers will come saying 'Where is the promise of his coming? All things continue as they were.' They deliberately overlook that the world was created by God's word and was once destroyed by water. By the same word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept until the day of judgement.
3.big: The God who created and once judged the world will certainly judge it again.

3.ctx: Peter answers the scoffers' question about delay. Decades had passed since Jesus' promise to return, and some were concluding it would never happen.
3.mean: Peter says with the Lord one day is as a thousand years. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away and the earth be exposed. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought they to be? They wait for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
3.big: The apparent delay in Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance.
3.diff: Verse 9 ('not wishing that any should perish') is often discussed alongside election. Reformed interpreters read it variously as God's genuine desire for all, distinct from his decree, or as referring to his elect ('you'); others see it as showing salvation is open to all. All agree it reveals God's patience and mercy.

3.ctx: The closing exhortations of what Peter presents as his last letter, drawing together the letter's themes of holy living, patience and guarding against error.
3.mean: Peter says to be diligent to be found without spot, at peace. Count the Lord's patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, whose letters contain some things hard to understand, which the ignorant twist to their destruction, as they do the other Scriptures. Beware of being carried away; grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
3.big: Believers must hold fast against error and keep growing in grace and knowledge of Christ.
3.diff: Verse 16 is notable for placing Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures', showing an early recognition of their authority.
